notes: Platform default discovery-question bank for the ArchAgentix intake flow. 30 organisation + 30 person + 20 project_business = 80. Authored data, never generated at runtime: AI assist proposes, a human accepts. Orgs store only their overrides (see packages/shared-core/src/store.js globalQuestions), which are merged over these rows at read time.

questions.question: How many people are in the organisation today, and how many are expected to use this system daily?
questions.whyItMatters: Drives the tenancy model, licensing tier, and whether SSO and role scoping are required from day one.

questions.question: How many business units or sites will the system serve, and are any of them outside your primary country?
questions.whyItMatters: Multi-site and cross-border units force regionalisation, data residency, and per-unit permissions before any feature work.

questions.question: What share of the workforce is technical (engineers, analysts) versus business-only users?
questions.whyItMatters: A mostly non-technical user base rules out self-hosted and config-heavy architectures.

questions.question: How is the organisation structured — functional, divisional, matrix, or network/remote-first?
questions.whyItMatters: Structure predicts how approval paths and data boundaries will actually behave under load.

questions.question: Which teams own software delivery today, and who owns the platform those teams run on?
questions.whyItMatters: Identifies whether a platform counterpart exists to operate what we build, or whether ownership is implicit.

questions.question: Is there a central IT or platform team, or does each unit procure and run its own tooling?
questions.whyItMatters: Federated procurement means one design cannot assume a single account, single identity, or single cloud.

questions.question: Who is accountable for the outcome of this project, and who can veto a technical decision?
questions.whyItMatters: Naming the veto holder prevents late redesigns discovered at the second approval layer.

questions.question: Which roles will operate the system day-to-day after go-live, and is that capacity funded?
questions.whyItMatters: Unfunded operations is the most common cause of a correct build degrading within a quarter.

questions.question: Who owns data quality and access decisions for the datasets this system will use?
questions.whyItMatters: Without a data owner, permission models are guessed and become the migration cost later.
choices: each team owns its own data

questions.question: How are technology decisions made here — committee, architect-led, team-autonomous, or ad hoc?
questions.whyItMatters: Determines whether a recommended architecture can be adopted as proposed or needs a consensus variant.

questions.question: What is the typical time from project approval to first production use?
questions.whyItMatters: Sets the honest upper bound on delivery cadence and whether an incremental release plan is viable.

questions.question: Which approvals are mandatory before something can reach production?
questions.whyItMatters: Each mandatory gate is a design constraint (audit trail, change control, evidence) not an afterthought.

questions.question: How do engineers get code from laptop to production today — describe the path and its friction.
questions.whyItMatters: Reveals whether we can plug into an existing pipeline or must stand one up as part of the work.

questions.question: What is the current testing and review practice — could another engineer safely review and revert a change?
questions.whyItMatters: Predicts how much isolation and verification the design must carry on the team's behalf.

questions.question: How is technical debt handled today — scheduled, dedicated, best effort, or untracked?
questions.whyItMatters: Debt discipline decides whether a pragmatic first release will be maintained or rewritten.

questions.question: Where does your system-of-record data live, and who else reads or writes it today?
questions.whyItMatters: Defines the integration and conflict surface; a system of record with silent writers is a data-quality risk.

questions.question: Is there a data classification or retention policy that applies to the data this project will hold?
questions.whyItMatters: Retention rules drive storage choice, deletion jobs, and backup design before anything else.

questions.question: How is master or reference data kept consistent across systems today?
questions.whyItMatters: If reference data is hand-copied, synchronisation becomes the core engineering problem.

questions.question: Which regulatory or contractual regimes constrain this system?
questions.whyItMatters: Each regime adds concrete requirements — consent, residency, auditability, breach timelines.

questions.question: What is the required data residency — must data stay inside a specific country or region?
questions.whyItMatters: Residency can eliminate cloud and provider options before features are considered.

questions.question: Has the organisation passed an external security audit, and what findings remain open?
questions.whyItMatters: Open findings usually name the exact controls this project will be judged against.

questions.question: List the tools already in use for identity, source control, CI/CD, issue tracking, and chat or alerting.
questions.whyItMatters: Establishes the baseline the design must connect to rather than a greenfield assumption.

questions.question: Which of those tools are contractual commitments you cannot replace, and which are simply habit?
questions.whyItMatters: Separates real constraints from preference, which changes how much of the stack we are free to choose.

questions.question: Is there an existing cloud account, enterprise subscription tier, or startup credit programme we should build on?
questions.whyItMatters: An existing commitment can make one provider clearly cheaper than any neutral recommendation.

questions.question: What systems must this exchange data with, and are those integrations API-first today?
questions.whyItMatters: Non-API integrations convert connector work into file-drop or manual-process design.

questions.question: Are there systems reachable only by file export/import, screen scraping, or a manual step?
questions.whyItMatters: Each manual step is a reliability hole the architecture must explicitly schedule, retry, and monitor.

questions.question: What is the largest volume of records or requests the system must absorb in a peak day or peak hour?
questions.whyItMatters: Order-of-magnitude load decides whether a queue, a batch pipeline, or a simple CRUD service is correct.

questions.question: How did the last significant system change land — adopted, worked around, or rejected?
questions.whyItMatters: History predicts the adoption plan we need; worked-around rollouts signal a training or incentives gap.

questions.question: Who will be trained, and is time and budget allocated for that training?
questions.whyItMatters: Unfunded training converts a delivered system into an unused one.

questions.question: What would make this project fail to be adopted even if it ships on time?
questions.whyItMatters: Elicits the political and workflow risks that no technical design can solve alone.

questions.question: What is your role, and how are you measured on this project?
questions.whyItMatters: What someone is measured on predicts which trade-offs they will accept.

questions.question: In this project, are you the decision-maker, the requester, the implementer, the operator, or an influencer?
questions.whyItMatters: Mismatch between who asks and who decides is the usual cause of requirements reversing mid-build.

questions.question: Who else will use this system that you are speaking for today, and have they been asked?
questions.whyItMatters: Reveals silent user groups whose needs only surface after go-live.

questions.question: What outcome would make you say this project paid for itself?
questions.whyItMatters: Gives the acceptance criterion the architecture should be optimised for.

questions.question: What are you personally risking if this succeeds or fails?
questions.whyItMatters: Personal stakes shape how much risk the sponsor will actually tolerate, independent of stated appetite.

questions.question: What is the primary driver behind this project?
questions.whyItMatters: Survival-driven projects justify shorter, less general designs; growth-driven ones justify platform investment.

questions.question: What is the hard deadline, and what happens if it is missed?
questions.whyItMatters: Distinguishes a real external constraint from a wishable date, which changes scope decisions.

questions.question: What is fixed and beyond your control?
questions.whyItMatters: Fixing the wrong corner of the scope triangle produces a plan that cannot be delivered as stated.

questions.question: Are there procurement or vendor policies that limit what can be bought, hosted, or opened to third parties?
questions.whyItMatters: Procurement rules can eliminate SaaS and managed services regardless of technical fit.

questions.question: How comfortable are you with cloud infrastructure — would you operate it, review changes to it, or expect it handed over?
questions.whyItMatters: Determines whether the design favours tunable primitives or managed services.

questions.question: Do you read code, and would you review an implementation before it ships?
questions.whyItMatters: Sets how much explanation and evidence the delivery process must carry.

questions.question: Who on your side can own this system after delivery, and at what depth?
questions.whyItMatters: Post-handoff ownership is the strongest predictor of whether the system survives year two.

questions.question: How many years have you worked in this domain, and what do newcomers usually get wrong?
questions.whyItMatters: Experienced answers name the non-obvious rules the design must respect.

questions.question: What is the one domain rule an outsider would break that nobody tells them?
questions.whyItMatters: Implicit domain rules are the most expensive late-stage requirement changes.

questions.question: Are you the last person who knows how the current process works, or is that knowledge written down?
questions.whyItMatters: Tribal-only knowledge adds a documentation and interview workstream to the project.

questions.question: Would you rather ship something reversible and slower, or irreversible and faster?
questions.whyItMatters: This single answer decides rollout design, data-model conservatism, and vendor lock-in tolerance.

questions.question: What is the worst acceptable outcome of an error this system makes?
questions.whyItMatters: Sets the required verification and human-in-the-loop depth.

questions.question: How do you feel about model-generated decisions reaching production without a human checking each one?
questions.whyItMatters: Determines whether approval gates belong in the core architecture or only in reporting.
choices: auto, audit after a confidence period

questions.question: How many hours per week can you give to this project for the next six weeks?
questions.whyItMatters: Access to the stakeholder limits iteration speed more than engineering capacity usually does.

questions.question: Who schedules the working sessions, and are you available in your stated timezone?
questions.whyItMatters: Unscheduled access becomes silent delay in the delivery plan.

questions.question: What else are you delivering this quarter that competes for the same hours?
questions.whyItMatters: Exposes the real capacity behind an enthusiastic commitment.

questions.question: How do you want to receive progress — written summary, scheduled call, or a live dashboard?
questions.whyItMatters: Mismatched reporting cadence reads as project drift even when delivery is on track.

questions.question: What is the fastest way to reach you when a blocking decision is needed?
questions.whyItMatters: Blocking decisions need a known short-latency channel or the schedule absorbs the wait.

questions.question: Do you want to see every intermediate step, or only checkpoints and outcomes?
questions.whyItMatters: Determines how much of the pipeline should be exposed as product surface versus internal logs.

questions.question: What have you already tried for this problem, and why did it stop working?
questions.whyItMatters: Failed attempts are free constraints; repeating them is the most avoidable cost.

questions.question: Is there a failed or abandoned attempt at this inside the organisation, and what killed it?
questions.whyItMatters: Organisational memory of a dead project determines whether the new one gets a second chance.

questions.question: What workarounds are people using today — spreadsheets, messaging threads, manual re-entry?
questions.whyItMatters: Live workarounds define the real workflow and the migration path users will accept.

questions.question: What single number moves if this works, and what is its current value?
questions.whyItMatters: A measurable baseline is the only defensible success test for the delivered system.

questions.question: What would your most sceptical colleague point to as proof this worked?
questions.whyItMatters: Surfaces the evidence standard the project will actually be judged by.

questions.question: At what point would you call this finished, and who signs that off?
questions.whyItMatters: Undefined acceptance turns delivery into an open-ended engagement.

questions.question: Describe the business in one paragraph: what is sold, to whom, and how value reaches the customer.
questions.whyItMatters: Domain shape determines entity model, transaction boundaries, and where the money is recorded.

questions.question: Which part of the operation generates most of the margin, and which part is the bottleneck?
questions.whyItMatters: Automating the bottleneck is worth far more than automating the margin generator.

questions.question: What is the single most expensive problem today, and what does it cost per month?
questions.whyItMatters: Quantified pain is the basis of every prioritisation trade-off in the build.

questions.question: Where does work wait, and how long does it wait?
questions.whyItMatters: Waiting is where latency, queueing, and status-visibility requirements actually come from.

questions.question: What alternatives have you evaluated, and why were they rejected?
questions.whyItMatters: Rejections carry the real selection criteria; re-proposing one loses credibility immediately.

questions.question: If nothing changes, what will you be doing instead in six months?
questions.whyItMatters: The credible do-nothing baseline defines the true value of shipping.

questions.question: What is the revenue model for this product?
questions.whyItMatters: Freemium in particular forces a plan and entitlement boundary into the data model from day one.

questions.question: Is there a free tier, and what specifically gates the upgrade — features, volume, seats, or support?
questions.whyItMatters: The gate determines where metering, quotas, and billing hooks must sit in the architecture.

questions.question: How much of this build are you willing to get wrong in exchange for speed — a throwaway prototype, a pilot with real users, or production-grade from day one?
questions.whyItMatters: Mismatched fidelity is the most common source of both overrun and regret.

questions.question: What is the approved budget range for this project, and does it also cover running costs after delivery?
questions.whyItMatters: Run-cost coverage decides between managed services with a monthly bill and cheaper self-hosted options.

questions.question: Do you have an existing cloud account and commitment, or is the cloud choice open?
questions.whyItMatters: Existing committed spend usually dominates any neutral technical recommendation.

questions.question: Must any component stay on-premise or in a private environment, and why?
questions.whyItMatters: One on-prem requirement converts a managed-service design into a hybrid one with its own release pipeline.

questions.question: Will users interact with this primarily through a browser application, and who are they — internal staff, customers, or both?
questions.whyItMatters: Internal versus customer browser surfaces differ completely on auth, branding, and accessibility requirements.

questions.question: Does the browser application need to work offline, on shared machines, or behind a corporate proxy?
questions.whyItMatters: Each of these rules out a plain SPA and pushes work into sync, session, or network design.

questions.question: Is a mobile application required, and is it for end customers or for your field and internal staff?
questions.whyItMatters: Customer apps carry store review and push-infrastructure obligations; internal apps usually do not.

questions.question: Which mobile platforms must be supported, and do you already ship an app to either store?
questions.whyItMatters: Existing apps inherit their teams, pipelines, and native constraints; a new app does not.

questions.question: Would a connectors-only solution that automates your existing tools meet this need, instead of a new application?
questions.whyItMatters: Connector-only scope can be a tenth of the cost, and the honest answer changes the whole proposal.

questions.question: Which systems would the connectors have to reach, and do they expose APIs, webhooks, or only exports today?
questions.whyItMatters: Determines whether integration is configuration or custom code, and which failure modes need retries.

questions.question: Is this a B2B, B2C, internal-only, or B2B2C product, and whose users must be isolated from each other?
questions.whyItMatters: B2B mandates multi-tenancy, per-tenant permissions, and admin self-service from the first commit.

questions.question: How do users authenticate to your existing systems today — a directory (AD / Entra / Okta / Google Workspace), SSO, email and password, or nothing?
questions.whyItMatters: The existing identity mechanism decides whether we integrate, migrate, or start from scratch — and how quickly users can be onboarded.
